# Java Container CPU Ergonomics

This example demonstrates how Java 25 observes CPU-related container limits and
how those limits affect JVM ergonomics.

The application is intentionally small. That is deliberate: this runbook
isolates one topic, CPU ergonomics, so the signal is not hidden behind
application framework behaviour, image layering, custom runtimes, CDS, startup
tuning, or container hardening.

Use this as a focused diagnostic example, not as a complete Java-in-containers
reference architecture. For a more holistic Spring Boot container example that
combines several workshop techniques, see
[Spring Boot Web Application with all examples in one place](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md).

The application prints values that are influenced by the JVM’s processor view:

- `Runtime.availableProcessors()`
- `OperatingSystemMXBean.getAvailableProcessors()`
- `ForkJoinPool.commonPool().getParallelism()`
- selected HotSpot VM options such as `UseContainerSupport`,
  `ActiveProcessorCount`, `ParallelGCThreads`, `ConcGCThreads`, and
  `CICompilerCount`
- cgroup CPU control files, when the process is running in a Linux container

This example is not a benchmark. It is a visibility exercise. Java 25 is
container-aware, but the useful workshop question is still: what did this JVM
detect, why did it choose those values, and which internal defaults changed
because of that detection?

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- inspect the JVM processor view and the cgroup CPU controls exposed to a
  container;
- build one application JAR and use it as the controlled input for host and
  container observations;
- compare the JVM’s reported defaults with and without a CPU quota; and
- explain why `ActiveProcessorCount` changes JVM ergonomics but not the CPU
  capacity enforced by the container runtime.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) runtime

### Oracle Container Registry access

Before pulling an Oracle Java base image, sign in to Oracle Container Registry
and accept the terms for the
[Oracle Java JDK repository](https://container-registry.oracle.com/ords/ocr/ba/java/jdk).

1. Accept the Oracle Container Registry terms.

2. Authenticate your container engine with your own Oracle Container Registry
   username and authentication token.

   Pass the token through standard input so it is neither recorded in shell
   history nor copied into the project or image layers. If you use Podman, use
   its equivalent `login --password-stdin` command.

   ```shell
   docker login container-registry.oracle.com \
     --username 'ALBERT.ATTARD@ORACLE.COM' \
     --password-stdin < ~/.ocr/auth-token
   ```

   This should print the login succeeded message.

   ```
   Login Succeeded!
   ```

3. Verify that the container engine can pull and run the Oracle Java JDK image.

   ```shell
   docker run --rm 'container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1' java --version
   ```

   Docker pulls the image if necessary, then prints the Java runtime version.

   ```
   java 25.0.4.1 2026-08-18 LTS
   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5, mixed mode, sharing)
   ```

## The artefacts to inspect

`Main` prints the JVM’s processor view, selected HotSpot ergonomics values, and
cgroup CPU control files.

```java
package demo;

import com.sun.management.HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.lang.management.GarbageCollectorMXBean;
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool;

public final class Main {

    private static final List<String> VM_OPTIONS = List.of(
            "UseContainerSupport",
            "ActiveProcessorCount",
            "ParallelGCThreads",
            "ConcGCThreads",
            "CICompilerCount"
    );

    private static final List<Path> CGROUP_FILES = List.of(
            Path.of("/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max"),
            Path.of("/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.weight"),
            Path.of("/sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus"),
            Path.of("/sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus.effective"),
            Path.of("/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_quota_us"),
            Path.of("/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_period_us"),
            Path.of("/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.shares")
    );

    static void main() {
        printSection("Java runtime");
        print("java.version", System.getProperty("java.version"));
        print("java.vm.name", System.getProperty("java.vm.name"));
        print("java.vm.version", System.getProperty("java.vm.version"));
        print("os.name", System.getProperty("os.name"));
        print("os.arch", System.getProperty("os.arch"));

        printSection("Processor view");
        print("Runtime.availableProcessors", Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors());
        print("OperatingSystemMXBean.availableProcessors", ManagementFactory.getOperatingSystemMXBean().getAvailableProcessors());
        print("ForkJoinPool.commonPool.parallelism", getParallelism());

        printSection("Garbage collectors");
        ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans().stream()
                .map(GarbageCollectorMXBean::getName)
                .forEach(name -> print("collector", name));

        printSection("Selected VM options");
        final HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean diagnostics = ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBean(HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean.class);
        VM_OPTIONS.forEach(option -> printVmOption(diagnostics, option));

        printSection("Container CPU control files");
        CGROUP_FILES.forEach(Main::printFileIfPresent);
    }

    private static int getParallelism() { /* Closed for brevity */ }

    private static void printVmOption(final HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean diagnostics, final String name) { /* Closed for brevity */ }

    private static void printFileIfPresent(final Path path) { /* Closed for brevity */ }

    private static void printSection(final String title) { /* Closed for brevity */ }

    private static void print(final String name, final Object value) { /* Closed for brevity */ }

    private Main() {}
}
```

The Dockerfile packages the JAR built later as `/opt/app/app.jar` in an Oracle
Java 25 runtime image.

```dockerfile
FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
WORKDIR "/opt/app"

ARG JAR_FILE="./target/libs/container-cpu-ergonomics-java-*.jar"
COPY ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "--module-path", ".", "--module", "demo"]
```

Together, these two artefacts make the relationship explicit: the same
application JAR is run on the host and then inside a container whose CPU
controls can change the JVM’s defaults.

## Build the application

Build the application before comparing local and container execution. The build
creates `target/libs/container-cpu-ergonomics-java-1.0.0.jar`, which is the
controlled input copied into the image in the next section. Using that same JAR
keeps the comparison focused on the JVM's execution environment.

1. Build the application

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name './target/libs'
   ```

   The application JAR file.

   ```
   ./target/libs
   └── container-cpu-ergonomics-java-1.0.0.jar

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

2. (*Optional*) Run the application directly on the host JVM first.

   This gives you a baseline outside Docker. The exact values depend on the
   machine, but the relationship between the values is what matters: the Java
   APIs expose the processor count the JVM is using, and several JVM defaults
   are derived from that count.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/libs/container-cpu-ergonomics-java-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

   The host JVM reports the processor view and selected ergonomics values.

   ```
   [Java runtime]
   java.version                                     25.0.4.1
   java.vm.name                                     Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
   java.vm.version                                  25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5
   os.name                                          Linux
   os.arch                                          amd64

   [Processor view]
   Runtime.availableProcessors                      8
   OperatingSystemMXBean.availableProcessors        8
   ForkJoinPool.commonPool.parallelism              7

   [Garbage collectors]
   collector                                        G1 Young Generation

   [Selected VM options]
   ```

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from this example directory. They use the JAR built in
[Build the application](#build-the-application) to isolate the effect of
container CPU controls from application packaging changes.

1. Build the example image.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
     --tag 'demo:container-cpu-ergonomics-java' \
     '.'
   ```

2. Run the image without an explicit CPU limit.

   This shows the JVM’s default processor view inside Docker before this runbook
   adds a quota. On many machines that means the JVM sees the container’s
   effective processor set, but the exact value can still vary with the host,
   Docker Desktop settings, cgroup version, and cpuset configuration.

   ```shell
   docker run --rm 'demo:container-cpu-ergonomics-java'
   ```

   The application prints Java, JVM, processor, GC, VM option, and cgroup CPU
   information from inside the container.

   ```
   [Java runtime]
   java.version                                     25.0.4.1
   java.vm.name                                     Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
   java.vm.version                                  25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5
   os.name                                          Linux
   os.arch                                          amd64

   [Processor view]
   Runtime.availableProcessors                      8
   OperatingSystemMXBean.availableProcessors        8
   ForkJoinPool.commonPool.parallelism              7

   [Garbage collectors]
   collector                                        G1 Young Generation
   collector                                        G1 Concurrent GC
   collector                                        G1 Old Generation

   [Selected VM options]
   UseContainerSupport                              true (DEFAULT)
   ActiveProcessorCount                             -1 (DEFAULT)
   ParallelGCThreads                                8 (DEFAULT)
   ConcGCThreads                                    2 (ERGONOMIC)
   CICompilerCount                                  4 (ERGONOMIC)

   [Container CPU control files]
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max                           max 100000
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.weight                        100
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus                       not present
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus.effective             not present
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_quota_us              not present
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_period_us             not present
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.shares                    not present
   ```

   In this run, the container is using cgroups v2. The `cpu.max` value
   `max 100000` means there is no CPU quota; the second field is the accounting
   period, expressed in microseconds. The `cpu.weight` value `100` is the
   default relative scheduling weight, not a CPU limit. Depending on the host
   and container runtime, cpuset information may be visible through files such
   as `cpuset.cpus.effective`; when present, that file shows the effective CPU
   set available to the container. In this output the cpuset files are not
   present, so the processor count must be inferred from the JVM-reported values
   or from the JVM container trace rather than from cpuset files. The
   `cpu.cfs_*` and `cpu.shares` files are cgroups v1 files, so their absence is
   expected on this cgroups v2 system.

### CPU quota

Now constrain the container to one CPU. The important value to watch is not the
raw host CPU count, but the JVM’s active processor count and the defaults
derived from it.

The `--cpus '1'` flag sets a cgroup CPU quota. For cgroups v2 this normally
appears as `100000 100000` in `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max`: a quota of 100000
microseconds per 100000 microsecond period, which is one CPU. HotSpot reads that
container metadata and uses it when computing its active processor count.

1. Run the container with 1 CPU

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --cpus '1' \
     'demo:container-cpu-ergonomics-java'
   ```

   With a one-CPU quota, Java should report an active processor count based on
   the quota and may use smaller default thread counts for JVM internals. The
   selected garbage collector can also change because HotSpot ergonomics are
   different for small CPU counts.

   ```
   [Java runtime]
   java.version                                     25.0.4.1
   java.vm.name                                     Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
   java.vm.version                                  25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5
   os.name                                          Linux
   os.arch                                          amd64

   [Processor view]
   Runtime.availableProcessors                      1
   OperatingSystemMXBean.availableProcessors        1
   ForkJoinPool.commonPool.parallelism              1

   [Garbage collectors]
   collector                                        Copy
   collector                                        MarkSweepCompact

   [Selected VM options]
   UseContainerSupport                              true (DEFAULT)
   ActiveProcessorCount                             -1 (DEFAULT)
   ParallelGCThreads                                0 (DEFAULT)
   ConcGCThreads                                    0 (DEFAULT)
   CICompilerCount                                  2 (ERGONOMIC)

   [Container CPU control files]
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max                           100000 100000
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.weight                        100
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus                       not present
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus.effective             not present
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_quota_us              not present
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_period_us             not present
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.shares                    not present
   ```

   The JVM can also print container detection details directly. This is often
   more useful than guessing from the application output alone: the trace
   explains which cgroup files were read and how quota divided by period became
   the active processor count.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --cpus '1' \
     --env JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS='-Xlog:os+container=trace' \
     'container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1' \
     java --version
   ```

   The JVM logs how it interprets the container’s CPU and memory control files.

   ```
   [0.000s][trace][os,container] OSContainer::init: Initializing Container Support
   [0.001s][debug][os,container] Detected optional pids controller entry in /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.controllers
   ```

### Active processor count override

`ActiveProcessorCount` overrides the processor count used by HotSpot ergonomics.
It does not give the container more CPU. That distinction matters: this option
can change JVM defaults and Java API results, but it cannot change the cgroup
quota enforced by the container runtime.

1. Run the container with 2 `ActiveProcessorCount`

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --cpus '1' \
     --env JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS='-XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2' \
     'demo:container-cpu-ergonomics-java'
   ```

   The JVM reports the override as a VM option set through `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`.
   The Java processor APIs now reflect the override, while the cgroup CPU quota
   remains unchanged. This is useful for experiments, but it is not a shortcut
   to more compute capacity.

   ```
   [Java runtime]
   java.version                                     25.0.4.1
   java.vm.name                                     Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
   java.vm.version                                  25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5
   os.name                                          Linux
   os.arch                                          amd64

   [Processor view]
   Runtime.availableProcessors                      2
   OperatingSystemMXBean.availableProcessors        2
   ForkJoinPool.commonPool.parallelism              1

   [Garbage collectors]
   collector                                        G1 Young Generation
   collector                                        G1 Concurrent GC
   collector                                        G1 Old Generation

   [Selected VM options]
   UseContainerSupport                              true (DEFAULT)
   ActiveProcessorCount                             2 (ENVIRON_VAR)
   ParallelGCThreads                                2 (DEFAULT)
   ConcGCThreads                                    1 (ERGONOMIC)
   CICompilerCount                                  2 (ERGONOMIC)

   [Container CPU control files]
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max                           100000 100000
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.weight                        100
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus                       not present
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus.effective             not present
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_quota_us              not present
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_period_us             not present
   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.shares                    not present
   Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2
   ```

If `ActiveProcessorCount` is set higher than the CPU capacity available to the
container, the JVM may size its GC, compiler and concurrency pools for more
processors than the container can use. The extra runnable threads compete for
the same limited CPU time and, under a CPU quota, may experience throttling.
This can delay work and increase latency, sometimes appearing as thread
starvation, although the issue is CPU contention rather than a lack of threads.
The override does not increase the container’s CPU entitlement.

- [The `java` command: container detection, `ActiveProcessorCount`, and unified logging](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/man/java.html)
- [JDK 25 `OperatingSystemMXBean` API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.management/java/lang/management/OperatingSystemMXBean.html)
- [Docker `run` reference: CPU options](https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/run/#cpu-period-constraint)

## Key takeaways and trade-offs

- CPU limits can change the JVM's active processor count and, in turn, the
  defaults used by JVM internals and Java concurrency libraries.
- The same JAR can expose materially different ergonomics values on the host
  and in a CPU-constrained container.
- `ActiveProcessorCount` is useful for controlled experiments and JVM tuning,
  but it does not increase the CPU entitlement enforced by the container
  runtime.
- Inspect cgroup files and `-Xlog:os+container=trace` before tuning. These
  observations are not evidence that a particular CPU setting is universally
  faster or production-ready. For complete Spring Boot container packaging
  concerns, continue with the
  [all-in-one-spring-boot](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md) example.
